newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Lufthansa profits down, Lauda stake sold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lufthansa profits down, Lauda stake sold.

text.p: German airline Lufthansa AG said on Wednesday its 1996 group income from ordinary activites was about 10 percent below the 1995 level of 756 million marks despite a five percent rise in total sales to almost 20 billion marks.

Lufthansa, which said it would release full corporate results on May 7, also said its transport revenues for the year were up 4.5 percent to 18.5 billion marks, backed by a 1.7 percent increase in the number of passengers aboard its planes.

But the airline said its results were hurt by a weak domestic market and lower prices for freight as well as higher fuel costs in the second half of 1996, noting the airline's fuel costs rose about 320 million marks last year.

The airline also said it would reduce its stake in Lauda Air to 20 percent from 39.7 percent in a deal to sell the stake to Austrian Airlines, which will allow Lufthansa to review possible cooperation deals in the country.
In addition to possible deals with Austrian Airlines and Lauda Air, Lufthansa said it may consider ventures with another Austrian airline, the regional carrier Tyrolean Airlines.

Austrian Airlines, meanwhile, said it would acquire a 36 percent stake in Lauda and that Lauda Air's founder and current majority owner, ex-racing car driver Niki Lauda, would retain 30 percent of the voting rights in the airline.
A Lufthansa official said the airline had no plans to sell the rest of its stake in Lauda Air. Terms of the deal were not immediately available.

In addition, Lufthansa said its supervisory board has approved a plan to restructure passenger services in a bid to prepare the airline for fierce competition expected to result from the impending liberalisation of European air traffic.

Lufthansa intends to restructure its passenger-service business by combining two divisions into one independent profit centre to be called "Passage". The reorganisation will cut management and administration by 10 percent.
The new unit will include sales, marketing, network management, cabin crews, pilots and ground staff and will account for 28,000 employees, or about 50 percent of the airline's total workforce.
The move marks the completion of a programme begun in 1994 and will take effect on April 1, the day when an "open skies" agreement will allow airlines to compete on all European routes.
